item.title: User data Telegram handed over to US law enforcement
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: A newly filed US federal court record includes a letter in which Telegram provided a user's phone number, user ID and IP address under a court order. Since September 2024, Telegram's privacy policy has allowed it to hand over IP addresses and phone numbers in criminal cases involving violations of its Terms of Service, no longer only for terror suspects, and the clause has no regional limit. As of 20 October, we had not seen a public response from Telegram to the filing.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including Telegram, Internet Archive, 404 Media

404 Media reported on 16 October that a newly filed document in a US federal court includes a letter from Telegram to US authorities, providing a user's phone number, user ID and IP address under a court order. According to CyberInsider, the letter is dated 4 September and was filed on 15 October in a criminal case in the US District Court for the Western District of Louisiana. The clause in Telegram's privacy policy on handing over IP addresses and phone numbers has no regional limit, so users outside the United States are subject to the same rules. As of 20 October, we had not seen a public response from Telegram to the filing.

404 Media's report is paywalled and we could read only its opening, and as of 20 October we could not find the court document itself, so the details of the letter come from CyberInsider's report. The IP address in the letter carries a timestamp in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) marking the account's last login. In the letter, Telegram describes the disclosure as voluntary and states that providing the data does not mean accepting US jurisdiction.

According to CyberInsider, the attachment contains only account and connection information and no message content, though that does not mean investigators obtained nothing else through other channels. The same report says Telegram usually needs a phone number to look up an account's non-public data. A username or numeric ID sometimes works when the account was previously actioned for content moderation, or when Telegram enabled additional logging after receiving a formal request. The letter does not say whether additional logging was enabled for this account.

Section 8.3 of Telegram's privacy policy, which we checked on 20 October, says that when Telegram receives a valid court order it first carries out a legal analysis and may disclose IP addresses and phone numbers to the relevant authorities. The order must confirm that the user is a suspect in a criminal case involving violations of Telegram's Terms of Service, and such disclosures are included in quarterly transparency reports. An archived copy of the page shows that before the change on 23 September 2024 the section covered only terror suspects and stated "So far, this has never happened".

Telegram's transparency reports are available only by querying an official bot from a Telegram account, and according to Meduza's explainer from October 2024, the bot returns data only for the country where the querying account is registered. 404 Media quoted the bot's reply in January 2025: from January to September 2024, Telegram fulfilled 14 US requests for IP addresses or phone numbers affecting 108 users, and 900 requests affecting 2,253 users over the full year. A crowdsourced dataset on GitHub, compiled from bot replies that users pasted in, lists 1,706 requests affecting 4,807 users for the United States in 2025. Telegram does not publish these figures on the web.

Perspective

According to Telegram's FAQ and privacy policy, both checked on 20 October, ordinary chats (cloud chats, including one-to-one chats and groups) are encrypted between the client and the server and stored on Telegram's servers. Secret Chats are end-to-end encrypted, meaning only the two participants' devices can decrypt them, and are not stored on the servers, only on the device each participant used to open the chat. The FAQ's section on data requests says the decryption keys for cloud chats are split across different jurisdictions, and that "To this day, we have disclosed 0 bytes of user messages to third parties, including governments". That section covers only message content, while the conditions for handing over IP addresses and phone numbers are in Section 8.3 of the privacy policy.

What Telegram provided in this letter was account data: a phone number, a user ID and an IP address. Section 5.2 of the privacy policy says that, for account security and to prevent spam and abuse, Telegram may collect IP addresses, the devices and apps used, and the history of username changes. Where collected, these records are kept for up to 12 months. Registering an account also requires a phone number.

We are a community based in Taiwan, where Article 77 of the Regulations for Administration of Mobile Broadband Businesses requires operators to record each subscriber's name, address and two identity document numbers, keep them for at least a year after the contract ends, and provide them when authorities make an inquiry under the law. From Section 8.3 of Telegram's privacy policy and this rule, we infer that once the number of an account registered with a Taiwanese number is handed over, Taiwanese authorities making an inquiry under the law can match the account to the subscriber.

Telegram does not publish country figures on the web, so the numbers for other places in Asia also come from the crowdsourced GitHub dataset, which counts requests for IP addresses or phone numbers that Telegram fulfilled. South Korea had 0 from January to September 2024, then 270 requests affecting 658 users from October to December 2024, and 2,101 requests affecting 5,454 users in 2025. Singapore had 4 requests affecting 4 users in 2024 and 14 affecting 16 in the first quarter of 2025, while Hong Kong and Japan appear only for January to September 2024, both at 0. Taiwan has no entry, though Meduza's October 2024 table lists it at 0 for January to September 2024, and we could not find figures for Taiwan, Hong Kong or Japan after September 2024, or for Singapore after the first quarter of 2025.

What a handed-over number can be matched to depends on what the carrier registered behind it, and the rules differ across Asia. In Hong Kong, under a regulation on SIM card registration that took effect on 1 September 2021, every SIM service plan and prepaid card has required real-name registration before activation since 1 March 2022, and individuals register their name in English and Chinese, date of birth, and Hong Kong identity card number with a copy of the card. In Singapore, the licence template that the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) issues to operators, which is not the text of a statute, requires them to register prepaid subscribers' name, address, identity document number and contact details and keep the register for at least 12 months after the service ends.

Article 32-4 of South Korea's Telecommunications Business Act, in the version in force from 1 October 2026, requires designated carriers to verify, with the subscriber's consent, that the person signing the contract is who they claim to be, and lets them ask for an identity card, including the mobile version, or a driver's licence. In Japan, Article 3 of the Act on Identity Confirmation by Mobile Voice Communications Carriers requires carriers to confirm an individual subscriber's name, address and date of birth at contract, and the 2026 White Paper on Information and Communications from the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications says the Act was amended in 2026 to require identity checks for data-only SIMs as well; we did not check when that amendment takes effect. We did not check whether the Korean and Japanese rules cover prepaid SIMs.

According to the FAQ, your phone number is visible by default only to people you have added to your own contacts, and the setting is under Settings > Privacy and Security > Phone Number. A 2019 post on Telegram's blog says that after setting who can see your number to Nobody, you can also limit who can find you by your number to your contacts (names in the current app may differ). According to the same post, strangers who add your number to their contacts then cannot match it to your profile, though the FAQ notes that people who already have your number saved can still see it. Usernames are always public, and the FAQ suggests not setting one if you do not want to be found through search.

For people who handle sensitive conversations, the FAQ recommends using Secret Chats with a self-destruct timer only in official or verifiable open-source apps, and turning on two-step verification and a passcode lock. To start a Secret Chat, open the other person's profile, tap "…" and choose Start Secret Chat, and note that Secret Chats disappear when you log out. Telegram's translation platform has a Traditional Chinese language pack that switches the interface through a share link, while the FAQ and privacy policy have no Chinese version. Our inference from Section 5.2 of the privacy policy and the phone number requirement at sign-up is that none of these steps means Telegram lacks the account's phone number, and whether IP addresses are collected depends on the circumstances described in Section 5.2.

item.title: Customer-list matching and conversation context in ChatGPT ads
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Advertisers on ChatGPT can upload lists of email addresses, phone numbers or mobile advertising IDs so that their ads reach only the people on those lists. Ads appear only on the Free and Go plans and began rolling out in Taiwan on 23 September. According to OpenAI's help page as of 20 October, ChatGPT still picks ads based on the current conversation after ad personalisation is turned off.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 15 sources, including OpenAI, 404 Media, Gizmodo

Advertisers on ChatGPT can upload lists of email addresses, phone numbers or mobile advertising IDs so that their ads are shown only to the people on those lists, 404 Media reported on 15 October. The feature appears on OpenAI's help page for advertisers under the name Custom Audiences. Ads appear only on the Free plan and the cheaper paid Go plan, not on Plus, Pro, Business or other plans, and began rolling out in Taiwan on 23 September. According to OpenAI's user help page as of 20 October, ChatGPT still picks ads based on the current conversation after ad personalisation is turned off.

According to the Custom Audiences help page, a list can contain email addresses, phone numbers, SHA-256 hashes of either, or Google Advertising IDs (GAID, the advertising identifier on Android phones). A hash is a one-way function that turns data into a fixed-length string. Advertisers can also upload raw, unhashed data, and uploaded files are usually deleted within 24 hours. OpenAI matches the list against ChatGPT users, and only the people matched count towards the audience.

A list can be used to show ads only to that audience, to exclude it, or to raise or lower the bid (what the advertiser is willing to pay for an impression or click) for it. Targeting an audience or adjusting bids requires at least 25,000 matched users, while an exclusion list can match fewer than 25,000. Ads Manager does not show which individuals were matched.

According to Gizmodo's account of the 404 Media report, 404 Media ran two ad campaigns on ChatGPT to test the system. Per the same account, it is unclear whether OpenAI hashes raw data after receiving it. The 404 Media report is paywalled, with only its first two paragraphs public, so the remaining details rely on Gizmodo's account.

According to OpenAI's user help page, OpenAI does not give advertisers users' conversations, memories, names, email addresses, precise location or IP addresses, and advertisers receive only aggregate performance figures such as views and clicks. If a user messages an advertiser through an ad, the advertiser can see those messages. Ads are not placed near conversations on sensitive topics such as personal health, mental health and politics, and are not shown in Temporary Chats or to accounts judged to belong to under-18s.

Perspective

Targeting ads with customer lists is common in the industry, and Google's Customer Match and Meta's customer list custom audiences are the same kind of feature. According to Meta's help page, Meta hashes a list before matching it, and according to Google's, Google does not receive the actual email addresses. The upload formats on OpenAI's help page include unhashed raw data. 404 Media also reported that ChatGPT ads are chosen based on the prompts users type.

Under OpenAI's Ad Tools Terms for advertisers, a list may contain only first-party data the advertiser collected itself, not data obtained from data brokers (companies that collect and resell personal data). Advertisers must warrant that they have given the required notice and obtained any necessary consent or other legal basis, and nothing in the terms describes how OpenAI verifies this. As of 20 October, the user help page has nothing on how to find out which advertisers' lists you are on. The ad menu has an "About this ad" option for seeing why a particular ad was shown, and the help page does not cover whether it reveals customer lists.

Our 26 September piece covered the pixel (tracking code advertisers install on their own sites), which sends browsing data from other sites back to OpenAI. Under OpenAI's privacy policy (the version for users outside the EEA, the UK and Switzerland), OpenAI may receive information from advertisers, such as purchases users make from them, and use it to show more relevant ads.

As of 20 October, mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau are not on OpenAI's list of countries and territories where ChatGPT is supported, nor on the list for its API. According to the ChatGPT list, using the service from outside the listed places may get an account blocked or suspended. ChatGPT ads began rolling out on 23 September in Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam and Taiwan, following earlier Asia-Pacific launches in Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea and India. According to OpenAI's help page, personalised ads are initially unavailable in the European Economic Area and Switzerland, with no other exceptions named, so no Asian market is set apart in the same way.

Customer lists are built from data advertisers hold about their own customers, and the rules in the places we checked differ. Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act has no provision specifically on advertising identifiers, real-time bidding or targeted ads, and the Chinese word for advertising (廣告) does not appear in its text. Its Article 20 does require a non-government entity that markets with personal data to stop once the person objects, and to offer a way to object the first time it markets to them. We read only the statute itself as of 18 October, not its enforcement rules or regulators' interpretations, and amendments dated 11 November 2025 are to take effect on a date set by the Executive Yuan.

Japan amended its Telecommunications Business Act in June 2022. According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications page, which we checked as of 18 October and which shows no update date, online information services such as messaging, social media, search and news that send user data to outside parties through tags or information-collection modules must give notice of or publish what is sent, or obtain consent or offer a way to stop it, though the rule does not ban targeted ads and does not cover corporate websites or personal blogs. South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission published a policy plan on 31 January 2024 to protect the online behavioural data used in targeted ads and set out to revise its targeted-advertising guidelines, though as of 18 October we could not find whether the revised guidelines are in force.

People on the Free or Go plan can go to Settings > Ad Controls in ChatGPT to turn off Personalize ads, and can also turn off Past chats and memory, a toggle that affects only ads. Ads data can be deleted in the same place, and is removed from OpenAI's servers within 30 days. According to the help page, people who cannot see these options in the mobile app should update it to the latest version. Turning off personalisation does not remove ads, and ChatGPT still picks them based on the current conversation.

People who do not want ads can switch to Plus or Pro, and the Free plan also has an ad-free option, though according to the help page its availability may vary by region and over time. The ad-free option comes with fewer messages per day and no access to tools such as image generation, and Go users have to switch back to Free to use it. In the Traditional Chinese version of the help page, the step "Change plan to go ad-free" appears as 「輕觸變更方案以享受 Go 無廣告體驗」, which reads as enjoying an ad-free Go plan, so follow the English wording. Because Temporary Chats do not show ads according to the help page, we infer that people who do not want a particular conversation to shape their ads can use a Temporary Chat.

Lists can contain email addresses, phone numbers and GAIDs, and as of 20 October OpenAI has not explained which account data it matches them against. If matching uses the email address and phone number registered to the ChatGPT account (our inference), a list built from a different address or number used for shopping or memberships may not match. Whether OpenAI will explain how it handles the raw data it receives, and whether turning off personalisation also excludes people from list matching, are the points to watch.

item.title: Implanted chips in Ledger hardware wallets
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 15 October Ledger confirmed that a criminal group had fitted genuine hardware wallets with parts that capture the recovery phrase during setup, then put them on the market through resellers in Southeast Asia. As of 13 October, the thefts Ledger had confirmed were all tied to devices sold by authorised reseller CryptoBilis, and reports of implants from other channels were unconfirmed. Ledger's Genuine Check cannot detect these implants, and Ledger advises anyone who bought and set up a device from CryptoBilis to move their assets to a new device and a new recovery phrase.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 20 sources, including Ledger, Ledger Support, Ledger Academy

Hardware wallet maker Ledger confirmed on its official blog on 15 October that a criminal group had spent months buying genuine Ledger devices. The group opened them and fitted hidden components that capture the recovery phrase (24 English words that can restore everything in the wallet) while the user sets the device up, then put the devices back on the market through resellers in Southeast Asia. According to the timeline from on-chain analytics firm Bitquery, the mass thefts began on 9 October. According to The Record, citing Ledger's 13 October statement, all confirmed thefts are linked to devices sold by CryptoBilis, an authorised Ledger reseller in Southeast Asia.

Cointelegraph reported that Ledger also said on 13 October it had not confirmed thefts from devices bought through other channels. Ledger's 15 October post says it has asked resellers in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong to pause sales. Ledger's Genuine Check, which connects to Ledger's servers to confirm that the secure element is original, cannot detect implants of this kind.

Ledger's 15 October post says there is no flaw in its chips, operating system or servers. In the post, Ledger describes the incident as a "localized distribution attack" that took place in the distribution channel after the devices left Ledger, and The Record also cites Ledger as saying the number of affected devices is limited. According to The Record, citing Ledger's 13 October statement, the implant reads what is shown on the screen, picks out the recovery phrase during setup and sends it out over the LTE mobile network through a built-in eSIM.

Tibane Labs, a blockchain research and development company, took apart two Nano X units bought from a Japanese auction site and a seller on Amazon Japan, and its page states that it did not test any CryptoBilis devices. The implant is a small computer soldered to the main board and wired to the screen's data line, and it makes no attempt to break the secure element (the chip that stores the private keys). Tibane Labs compared three versions and found that the dedicated antenna on the latest one is printed with a part number and version number, from which it inferred that the implant is mass-produced.

As of 20 October, Ledger has not disclosed the affected models, batches, number of people or amounts. Bitquery counted 335 wallets and US$102 million drained as of 16 October, and the US$92.9 million in earlier reports from crypto.news and others was an earlier Bitquery figure. Bitquery's page says the on-chain record points to a single actor holding the keys to every drained wallet, but the chain shows only transfers, not where the keys leaked from.

Zero Day, a security journalist's newsletter, reported on 13 October on claims of implants in devices bought outside CryptoBilis. An unnamed Japanese researcher told Zero Day he had bought ten units in total from unauthorised online sellers, the earliest in March, and every one had an implant. The same report cites a post on X by a German buyer who said he bought implanted Nano X units from MediaMarkt, which Ledger lists as an authorised reseller in Germany, at two of its stores. As of 20 October, Ledger has not confirmed these accounts.

The Record quotes Ledger's 13 October statement as saying it is "also reviewing reports of implants in other signers and locations". According to crypto.news, MediaMarkt paused sales with Ledger's agreement. Ledger said it had received no reports of lost funds in the German cases and had not established whether the German reports were related to the others. Ledger's 15 October post says it sent people to buy and open devices in markets including Germany and that "Every unit examined was clean", without giving the number of units examined.

Perspective

According to Ledger's educational site Ledger Academy, the private keys are stored in the secure element. The device generates the recovery phrase at initialisation and displays it only that once. Ledger's support page on checking hardware integrity says Genuine Check verifies a key written into the secure element at the factory, which keeps out counterfeits. The same page notes that as long as the original secure element is intact, Genuine Check cannot detect physical modifications such as implants.

The implant described by The Record and Tibane Labs leaves the secure element alone and reads the recovery phrase off the screen's data line at the moment it is displayed. The hardware integrity page says that on the Nano X and Nano S Plus, the secure element checks the main microcontroller's firmware at startup and shows a warning if it has been altered. The other check the page lists is opening the case and comparing the inside with Ledger's official photos to make sure no extra chip has been added. Tibane Labs' page says the device itself cannot detect the implant, and that the latest version is painted the same colour as the original circuit board.

According to The Record, citing Ledger's 13 October statement, anyone with a CryptoBilis device that has not been set up should leave it that way and contact support. Those who have already set one up should move their assets to a new device and a new recovery phrase as soon as possible, and should not enter or restore any recovery phrase on a device bought from CryptoBilis. Victims should contact Ledger and local police before deciding whether to open the device or send it anywhere.

For people who bought a Nano X of unknown origin through other channels and have already set it up, Ledger had made no recommendation to change the recovery phrase as of 20 October. Tibane Labs' page recommends replacing any recovery phrase that was shown on a Nano X of unknown origin, generating a new one on a trusted device and moving the assets to it. The page also says a recovery phrase shown on a modified screen should be treated as leaked even if the device has never been online. According to the hardware integrity page, people comfortable with hardware can open the case and compare, but damage from opening it is not covered by the warranty.

People who have not bought a device yet, or have just received one, can follow the purchasing guidance on Ledger's support site. Do not use a device whose packaging looks opened or resealed, or that comes with a card already filled in with a recovery phrase, and contact support instead. Ledger recommends buying from its official store or an authorised reseller, and as of 20 October its reseller page lists six resellers in Taiwan and five in Hong Kong, with no pause marked on the Hong Kong entries. These support pages had no Traditional Chinese version as of 20 October.

Elsewhere in Asia, the same reseller page lists six resellers in Singapore, only Amazon Japan for Japan, and no entry for mainland China. As of 20 October it marks "Sales temporarily paused" only on CryptoBilis in Indonesia and Malaysia and on some online shops in Malaysia and the Philippines. According to Cointelegraph, which reported a social media post from Ledger, the 13 October request covered resellers in Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Hong Kong, but the Hong Kong and Singapore entries carry no pause label. As of 20 October, Ledger's list of official Amazon stores includes Japan and Singapore but not Taiwan, Hong Kong or mainland China.

The crypto rules we found in Taiwan, Hong Kong, mainland China, Japan and Singapore concern service providers, trading platforms or crypto businesses, and as of 20 October we found no provision on selling, importing or owning hardware wallets themselves (which does not mean none exists). Taiwan's Virtual Asset Service Act, passed by the Legislative Yuan on 30 June 2026 with a start date still to be set by the Executive Yuan, covers seven kinds of virtual asset service providers, including exchanges, trading platforms, transfer services and custodians. The press release from the Securities and Futures Bureau of the Financial Supervisory Commission does not mention wallets or self-custody.

Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) requires centralised virtual asset trading platforms doing business in Hong Kong or marketing to Hong Kong investors to be licensed, and its page does not mention wallets. The 2020 English translation of Japan's Payment Services Act counts managing crypto-assets on behalf of another person as a crypto-asset exchange service; we did not check later amendments, and the translation does not mention wallets. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) brought custody of digital payment tokens under its Payment Services Act from April 2024, and its page does not mention wallets either.

In mainland China, eight departments including the People's Bank of China issued a notice on further preventing and dealing with risks related to virtual currency on 6 February 2026. We read only a media reprint of its full text, which treats domestic virtual currency exchange and trading as suspected illegal financial activity and says that civil acts of investing in virtual currency that violate public order and good morals are void, but it does not mention wallets.

CryptoBilis and MediaMarkt are both on Ledger's list of authorised resellers, and Ledger Academy's buying guide says "no global supply chain is entirely immune". Our inference is that buying through authorised channels lowers the risk but cannot guarantee a device has not been tampered with.

In its 15 October post, Ledger asks resellers to stop placing devices on shelves and in display cases and to hand them to buyers directly from stock, and repeats that returned devices must never be resold. The same post says Ledger will publish fuller technical details and is developing product-level protections. What comes of these two, and whether Ledger widens the scope of what it has confirmed, are the things to watch next.

item.title: End-to-end Encrypted Chats and Confidential Computing in Brave Leo
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: From 15 October, Brave's AI assistant Leo encrypts chats with the GLM 5.3 Flash model in the browser and decrypts them only inside hardware-isolated enclaves. Other models are not covered. As of 20 October, Brave's servers still check the enclaves' attestations for the browser, and we found no statement of iOS support.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 19 sources, including Brave, GitHub, Hugging Face

Brave announced on 15 October that chats between its AI assistant Leo and the GLM 5.3 Flash model are now end-to-end encrypted. GLM 5.3 Flash is a model whose weights Z.ai publishes under the MIT licence. Chats are encrypted in the browser and decrypted and answered only inside trusted execution environments (TEEs, compute areas in the processor and GPU isolated from the rest of the host) run by NEAR AI. The encryption applies only when you pick GLM 5.3 Flash by hand in Leo's model menu, Leo's other models are not covered, and as of 20 October GLM 5.3 Flash is still labelled as in testing.

According to the blog, the feature is available to all Brave users in the release version and in the Nightly and Beta test channels, but the blog does not say which platforms. The GitHub development issue is tagged only for desktop and Android, and as of 20 October we found no statement of support for the iPhone version.

According to Brave's blog, the browser encrypts each prompt, and any web page shared with Leo, with Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP), a standard from the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), and the decryption keys exist only inside the TEE. Encrypted messages go first to Brave's own AI Gateway and are then relayed to NEAR AI. Brave can see the user's IP address but not the content, NEAR AI's TEE decrypts the content without seeing the IP address, and according to the blog neither NEAR AI nor the cloud host operators can read inside the enclave. Each turn re-encrypts the whole conversation with a new one-time key, and the history stays only on the user's device, stored by neither Brave nor NEAR AI.

The blog then describes the checks before deployment, under which every NEAR AI deployment has to pass Brave's verifier before it is approved. The checks cover attestations signed by Intel and Nvidia (credentials signed by the hardware that prove the enclave is genuine and record which program runs inside it), and a rebuild from source to confirm it matches the program in production. The AI Gateway checks again before relaying each message, accepts verification results no more than an hour old, and does not relay anything that fails. The verifier, near-tee-verifier, is released under an open-source licence, and anyone with a NEAR AI API key can run it against the live service.

Brave trialled a first version in Nightly in November 2025, and according to the blog that protection rested on policy, with the checks also requiring trust in Brave. The new verifier is public and anyone with an API key can run it. As of 20 October, the browser-side check is still handled by Brave's servers.

As of 20 October, the help centre has no article on end-to-end encryption with GLM 5.3 Flash. Leo's model page still lists GLM 4.7 Flash and says all models are run by Brave itself. The development issue is marked to be left out of release notes, and none of the platforms' release notes mention end-to-end encryption.

Perspective

A typical AI chat service decrypts prompts on its servers, so the operator can technically read them and users have to rely on the privacy policy. OHTTP splits "who is asking" from "what is asked" between two parties, so the relay knows only the IP address and the processor sees only the content. TEEs are designed so that even the host operator cannot read the enclave's memory, and attestation lets outsiders confirm that what runs inside is a published program. Brave's blog describes Leo's new approach as a move from policy promises to cryptographic proof.

According to the blog, at launch on 15 October the browser still relied on Brave's AI Gateway for the checks, with the browser to verify the hardware attestations directly in later stages. Also according to the blog, the whole chain ultimately rests on trust in Intel and Nvidia, dstack (the TEE's operating system), Sigstore for build records, GitHub, Hugging Face and public DNS. The near-tee-verifier documentation adds a caveat that a rebuild proves only that the live program comes from a specified version, not that the version has no backdoor. The inference software that runs the model is a third-party package, which according to the blog and the near-tee-verifier documentation is not rebuilt from source but pinned to a version through deployment records covered by the hardware attestation.

In TEE.fail, a paper accepted at the security conference IEEE S&P 2026, researchers attached an interposition device to a server's DDR5 memory bus and, in some cases, extracted the key that Intel TDX (the TEE technology on Intel processors) uses to sign attestations. Attestations forged with that key can pass verification, and the key can also be used to break confidential computing on Nvidia GPUs. According to the research site, the attack requires physical access to the server, and Intel does not count such physical attacks among the threats TDX is meant to defend against. The researchers also write that, to their knowledge, it has not been exploited in the wild.

Another section of the research site demonstrates against dstack that a malicious server provider can forge all the attestations and can also borrow attestations from Nvidia GPUs elsewhere. The site's advice to dstack users is to be aware that they have to trust the operator who actually manages the TDX hardware. The paper does not analyse the Brave and NEAR AI deployment, and when we searched on 20 October we found no independent analysis of Leo.

According to the near-tee-verifier documentation, the GPU attestation is not bound into the TDX attestation, so there is no way to confirm which GPU an answer came from. Closing that gap would need NEAR AI to add the binding between the two.

In mainland China, GreatFire's last test, on 18 October, found brave.com 100% blocked, with interference recorded since 13 May 2017, and its most recent valid test of laptop-updates.brave.com, used for downloads and updates, was also blocked. Leo's backend, ai-chat.bsg.brave.com, has no measurements, since OONI's public API holds no Web Connectivity measurement of it from China between 20 July and 20 October and GreatFire has not tested it, so we found no direct evidence on whether Leo is reachable there. Apple's iTunes lookup API returns no Brave listing in the mainland China App Store (we did not check Google Play), which is a lookup result rather than an announcement of removal by Brave or Apple.

The same lookup finds Brave 1.96 (6 October) in the Taiwan, Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea and Singapore App Stores. Brave's help centre has no clause restricting where Leo can be used and does not say whether Leo is offered in mainland China, and the Leo page says Leo is available on desktop and mobile. Brave's development branch already has strings for Leo's end-to-end encryption in Traditional Chinese, Simplified Chinese, Japanese and Korean, though translation files in the development branch do not mean the release version offers them.

People who want to use an AI chat for text or web pages they would rather the service provider not read can open Leo in Brave on desktop or Android and choose GLM 5.3 Flash from the model menu. According to the English strings in the source code's development branch, the model menu shows "Verifiably Private With NEAR AI TEE" next to GLM 5.3 Flash, and answers carry a "Verified" badge. Inferring from the source code and the blog, the badge reflects the result of Brave's server-side check, and as of 20 October the browser itself does not yet verify the attestations. Leo needs no account, and the help page mentions a usage limit on the free tier without giving a number.

Brave has not published which languages Leo's answers support, and the GLM 5.3 Flash model card on Hugging Face lists English and Chinese. According to the blog, the encryption covers only the chat content, and Brave, which relays the messages, can still see the IP address. Search queries generated by the model also leave the TEE and go to Brave Search (not tied to the IP address).

item.title: Senate second reading of Canada's Bill C-22 and providers' responses
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Canada's Bill C-22 on lawful access went to second reading debate in the Senate on 8 October and, as of 18 October, had not passed second reading. A Signal vice president said at a panel that Signal would have to leave Canada if ordered to collect more metadata, while the public safety minister's office said the bill does not require decrypting end-to-end encrypted information. Readers outside Canada do not need to change any settings now.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 10 sources, including Parliament of Canada, Senate of Canada, Public Safety Canada

Canada's Lawful Access Act, Bill C-22, passed third reading in the House of Commons in June, and the Senate adjourned after its second reading debate on 8 October, with its next sitting on 20 October. According to LEGISinfo, Parliament's bill database, as of 18 October the bill had not passed second reading, and there was no record of it being referred to a committee or receiving Royal Assent (the Governor General's signature that makes it law). Between 4 and 16 October, Signal, the censorship circumvention tool Psiphon and Citizen Lab, a research lab at the University of Toronto, set out their objections in public, while the senator sponsoring the bill for the government (the sponsor) explained its safeguards in a second reading speech. The bill has not passed and the providers' exits are conditional, so in our assessment readers outside Canada do not need to change any settings now.

Signal's vice president of strategy and global affairs spoke at a panel held by the Internet Society's Canada chapter on 5 October, and The Globe and Mail reported it the next day. According to the report, the vice president argued that legal protection for encryption has to cover more than decryption with keys, and that being required to make major changes to the software would equally defeat the purpose of encryption. Signal keeps only users' phone numbers, the date they joined and their last login information, and if ordered to collect more metadata (records about communications rather than their content) and keep it for up to six months, it would have to leave Canada. As of 18 October, Signal's blog and Bluesky account had not published a written statement on C-22.

Psiphon told The Globe and Mail on 2 October that it had begun drawing up plans to move its operations out of Canada if the bill passes as it stands. In a written reply, the company's vice president wrote that every line of its open source code is public, so any access capability the bill required would be visible to the whole world, including the authoritarian governments its users are trying to evade. A senior researcher at Citizen Lab argued in an opinion piece in the same newspaper on 9 October that no design lets law enforcement in while giving other attackers no chance to exploit it, and Citizen Lab republished a summary on its website on 16 October.

According to the sponsor's second reading speech on 8 October, the new law in Part 2 of the bill, which regulates providers' technical capabilities, does not in itself give law enforcement or the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) new powers to obtain information. Ministerial orders need approval from the Intelligence Commissioner, an independent official who reviews intelligence authorisations, are subject to independent review and last at most two years. Metadata retention is limited to specified categories for up to six months and excludes communications content and browsing history. A spokesperson for the public safety minister's office told The Globe and Mail that the bill explicitly does not require decrypting end-to-end encrypted information, and does not allow or compel providers to introduce systemic vulnerabilities or backdoors.

Perspective

According to Public Safety Canada's committee briefing notes from May, a provider that assesses it cannot meet a requirement without introducing a systemic vulnerability (one that affects a whole class of products or many users, not just a single target) does not have to comply, and the government uses the term to mark out what providers need not do. The sponsor also told the Senate that the committee needs to hear technical evidence on how the term works when a capability described as targeted could affect an entire product or update system. A senator quoted Psiphon's view that any legally mandated access mechanism in open source software would be public and could not be limited to Canadian agencies or a single investigation.

Oversight is another point of dispute. In the debate, one senator criticised the exclusion of ministerial orders from the Statutory Instruments Act, the law that sends regulations to Parliament for scrutiny, and another cited a joint brief from Citizen Lab and a civil liberties group saying the bill's obligations can be imposed without judicial authorisation. The sponsor said in the speech that orders and supporting material must go to the National Security and Intelligence Review Agency (NSIRA), an independent body that reviews intelligence and security agencies, and cited support for the bill from a representative of police organisations.

According to Public Safety Canada's briefing notes, Australia has a similar safeguard. Australia's Assistance and Access Act of 2018 likewise provides that a technical capability notice, a written order requiring a provider to build a particular capability, may not require it to build a systemic weakness or systemic vulnerability. The Australian law defines a systemic weakness as one that affects a whole class of technology, excluding a weakness selectively introduced to target a particular person unless it would jeopardise the security of other people's information. In the opinion piece, the Citizen Lab researcher cited Australia's experience, including one company's statement that lost trust caused economic losses of about A$1 billion.

When comparing approaches, it is worth asking who approves an order, whether a court is involved and whether providers may disclose that an order exists. Who decides what counts as a systemic vulnerability, and the scope and duration of metadata retention, can also be compared. Another question is whether the investigative goals behind the policy can be met without weakening encryption.

In Hong Kong, according to the government's 2020 announcement of the implementation rules for Article 43 of the National Security Law, officers may, under specific circumstances, apply to a magistrate for a warrant authorising police to request identification records or decryption assistance from a service provider, and all applications to intercept communications must be approved by the Chief Executive. In mainland China, Article 18 of the Counter-Terrorism Law requires telecom operators and internet service providers to give public security and state security organs technical interfaces and decryption support for preventing and investigating terrorism. Article 18 itself names no approving body and has no exception like Canada's systemic vulnerability. For mainland China we checked only Article 18, and for both places we have not looked into whether providers may disclose a request they receive.

Signal's and Psiphon's exits are both conditional, and as of 18 October neither had announced a date. The Senate's second reading vote after it resumes on 20 October, and which committee the bill goes to, are the next steps to watch. How readers in Canada will be affected depends on the bill's final text and the providers' decisions.

item.title: Automatic phone number verification on Android and the linking of Google accounts
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Android phones verify phone numbers automatically by default and add them to every Google Account signed in on the phone, including work and secondary accounts. Verification can be turned off in settings, but according to Android Authority, numbers already added have to be removed from each account one by one. As of 18 October, we had not seen a public response from Google.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 13 sources, including Android Help, Android 說明, Android Authority

Android Authority reported on 14 October that Android phones verify phone numbers automatically and add them to every Google Account signed in on the phone, including work and secondary accounts. According to Google's Android Help page "Manage phone number verification on your device", the feature is on by default and applies to both current and future accounts and phone numbers. Android Authority reports that the on-by-default wording was added to the page between August and October 2025, and we could not find an earlier version of the page to compare. Android Authority has asked Google for comment, and as of 18 October we had not seen a public response.

Any Google Account signed in on an Android phone gets the number, so people who use several accounts on one phone end up with those accounts tied together by the same number. Per the same help page, verification keeps features such as signing in with a phone number, account recovery, emergency location, finding a lost device, RCS (the newer messaging format that succeeds SMS) and Quick Share working. Google and the carrier periodically reverify the numbers, and carrier charges may apply.

Two Google Play services help pages describe how Google Play services may send and access SMS messages and access call logs in the background to discover and verify the number. The English versions of both pages read "If you opt-in to phone number verification", while the Traditional Chinese versions render it as 如果您啟用電話號碼驗證功能 ("if you turn on phone number verification"). The opt-in wording does not match the on-by-default description, and neither page explains the difference.

The Google Account Help page "Change the phone number on your account & how it's used" lists three uses for a number once it is on an account: sign-in and account recovery, helping people find and contact you through Google services, and showing more relevant ads when "Better ads & Google services" is on. Google's privacy policy, in effect from 16 October, lists the same uses, and the account help page adds that Google does not sell personal information, including phone numbers.

According to the device help page, turning on phone number verification also turns on Better sharing on Google, which makes it easier for people to send photos and start video calls through the number. With several accounts on the same phone, this setting is on for only one of them.

Perspective

Several accounts on one phone are often a personal and a work account, or an account deliberately kept apart from someone's real identity. In the help page's example, a newly added Google Account is linked to every number on the device, and a new number is added to every account. Our inference is that once a number is on an account, anyone who can obtain both the Google Account data and the carrier's registration records, such as authorities making a lawful request, can match the account to the identity registered to the number. Real-name rules for SIM cards differ from place to place, and so does how much identity data sits behind a number.

We are a community based in Taiwan, where Article 77 of the Regulations for Administration of Mobile Broadband Businesses (amended 3 September 2019) requires operators to record each subscriber's name, address and two identity document numbers before activation, prepaid cards included. Operators must keep the records for at least a year after the contract ends and provide them when authorities make an inquiry under the law. In Hong Kong, the Telecommunications (Registration of SIM Cards) Regulation took effect on 1 September 2021, and since 1 March 2022 every SIM service plan and prepaid card has required real-name registration before activation. According to the Office of the Communications Authority, individuals register their name in English and Chinese, date of birth, Hong Kong identity card number and a copy of the card.

In Singapore, the requirement is set in the licence template that the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) issues to operators, which is not the text of a statute. Version 10 of the template, dated 1 December 2025, requires operators to register prepaid subscribers' name, address, identity document number, contact details and service identifier, and to check and copy the identity document for purchases made in Singapore. The register must be kept for at least 12 months after the service ends, and operators may not provide prepaid service to anyone under 15.

According to Google's help page, account recovery, signing in with a phone number, emergency location and other features depend on verification, so turning it off may affect them, which is our inference from the help page. Google's privacy policy lists carrier name and phone number among the mobile network information it collects. Based on that list, we infer that Google may still obtain the phone's number after verification is turned off and the number is removed. We could not find out whether Google links the accounts internally as a result.

If you are signed in to several accounts on one Android phone and do not want them tied together by the number, go to Settings → Google → All services → Privacy & security → Phone number verification and turn it off. According to Android Authority, turning it off only stops future linking, and numbers already added have to be deleted from each account under Personal info → Phone (Google's help page does not say whether turning it off removes them). You can keep the number on the account you rely on for recovery and remove it only from the accounts you want kept apart, which is our inference. The device and Google Account help pages both have Traditional Chinese versions, whose footers note that they may contain AI-translated content.

Android Authority cites user reports on Reddit that the toggle switched back on after being turned off, which the author had not reproduced by publication. Given those reports, we suggest checking the setting again some time after turning it off.

item.title: The passkey attestation debate
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 10 October a commentary argued against using passkeys because sites can use attestation to restrict which devices and software people may use, and on 14 October an author published a response. Both agree that passkeys are, in most cases, bound to a domain and resist phishing; they disagree on whether attestation will become a restriction, and on whether to keep using passkeys or switch to something else.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 23 sources, including Non-Functional, scotthelme.co.uk, W3C

Passkeys replace passwords with the screen lock on a phone or computer, and each passkey works only on the domain where it was created. A commentary published on Substack on 10 October under the title "Passkeys are a trap. Do not use them." argues that sites can use attestation, a mechanism by which the device or software storing a key shows a site where it comes from, to gradually restrict which devices and software people can use.

On 14 October an author responded with "Passkeys Are Not a Trap", arguing that the synced passkeys most people use, stored in a password manager and synced between devices, provide no attestation. Both pieces agree that passwords are not secure and that passkeys are, in most cases, bound to a domain; the dispute centres on attestation, and on whether to keep using passkeys or switch to something else.

The commentary's author first points out that things differing in whether they can be copied, and in whether they live in hardware or software, are all called passkeys, and speculates that the name was chosen so users would not look closely. The author's core argument is that sites can use attestation to confirm a user has an approved password manager, and once most users are unaffected, start rejecting passkeys without attestation. According to the author, attestation requires the crypto processor, password manager, operating system and firmware all to pass checks, so people who install LineageOS to keep an old phone going, for example, might fail. The author also writes that attestation has legitimate uses and that most sites do not require it at the time of writing, recommends one-time codes from an authenticator app (TOTP) in the main text, and in a note at the end separately recommends hardware security keys such as YubiKey.

The response's author writes that even if a site asks for attestation, synced passkeys in iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password or Bitwarden return only "none", meaning no attestation. By this author's reasoning, a consumer site that accepted only attested passkeys would immediately lock out almost all of its users. According to the response, attestation tells a site only the make and model of the authenticator (the phone, password manager or security key that stores the key), and does not include the operating system, browser, extensions, firmware version or whether the phone is jailbroken. To the YubiKey recommendation, the author replies that every YubiKey ships with an attestation certificate signed by Yubico, so people worried about attestation would be pushed towards it.

Perspective

The WebAuthn Level 3 specification, published by the W3C in August 2026, sets the default for attestation to none and leaves the attestation format to the authenticator. A site can state a preference and decide under its own policy which attestations to accept. The specification identifies authenticator types by AAGUID, a 128-bit identifier for an authenticator model, and its privacy considerations include the risk that attestation certificates are used to track users, with mitigations such as sharing one certificate across a large batch of devices or using an anonymization CA. In the Android SafetyNet format, which the specification already lists as deprecated, the attestation includes information on the platform's health; according to the response, attestation does not include the state of the operating system, but in our reading that depends on the format.

Under the same specification, enterprise attestation, which may include information that identifies an individual device, is provided only when the browser or authenticator settings allow it for that site. Under the digital identity guidelines that the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) issues for federal agencies (SP 800-63-4), public-facing services should not reject synced passkeys because attestation is unavailable, since that could push users towards methods that are easy to phish. The same guidelines also recommend that services use attestation, when present, to decide how much to trust an authenticator, and that internal federal systems implement it. Services can also restrict synced passkeys using the backup eligibility flag, a field showing whether a key can be synced or backed up.

The response's author starts from the situation in October 2026, when most consumer sites do not require attestation and the major sync services do not provide it. The same author writes that if consumer sites really did start requiring attestation, it would be worth objecting loudly. The commentary's concern is where things go next, and its author reasons that only the small number of people running modified systems would be affected, so sites could tighten their requirements gradually without drawing attention.

The response's author writes that TOTP codes can be typed into a fake site, and that phishing tools such as Evilginx, a relay server placed between the user and the real site, can forward passwords and codes in real time. Under NIST's guidelines, one-time passwords that must be entered by hand do not count as phishing-resistant authenticators, while properly configured synced passkeys do. In the commentary's main text, the author recommends TOTP because users can freely choose their software and hardware. In the note at the end, the author mentions that passkeys are, in most cases, bound to a domain and can withstand man-in-the-middle attacks, and recommends security keys.

Both pieces touch only briefly on changing devices and moving passkeys: the commentary's author mentions needing to take keys along when changing phones, and the response's author suggests that people who want to move them choose a provider that supports it. According to the FIDO Alliance, synced passkeys are end-to-end encrypted as they sync between devices. Per the two companies' help pages, Apple recovers passkeys through iCloud Keychain escrow, while Google requires the Google Password Manager PIN or the screen lock of an old Android device.

As of 18 October, Bitwarden and 1Password can export passkeys directly using the FIDO Alliance's Credential Exchange Protocol (CXP), which is still a draft. Both require iOS 26 or Android 14 or later (Bitwarden's export page lists Android 10 or later), and the receiving app must support it too. KeePassXC, by contrast, exports passkeys to an unencrypted file.

In Japan, the Financial Services Agency (FSA) amended its supervisory guidelines for securities firms, effective 15 October 2025, to look for phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, turned on by default, for important operations such as logging in, withdrawing funds and changing the bank account for withdrawals. Passkeys and PKI-based authentication appear in the text only as examples, and firms are not limited to passkeys. According to materials from a November 2025 exchange of views between the FSA and the Japan Securities Dealers Association, securities firms are expected, in principle, to have this in place by the end of June 2026.

In Singapore, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Association of Banks in Singapore announced on 9 July 2024 that major retail banks would progressively phase out one-time passwords for login by digital token users within three months, with no mention of passkeys or FIDO in the press release. Singpass, the government's digital identity, opened a beta of passkey login on 1 July 2026, starting with iPhone, with Android to follow and existing login methods kept; in guidance from the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA), passkeys are listed as phishing-resistant and SMS one-time passwords are not. In Taiwan, the Ministry of Digital Affairs joined the FIDO Alliance as a government member in January 2023, the second government body to do so after the Ministry of the Interior, and the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) has promoted a standardised mobile identity mechanism for finance since 2021, renamed Finance Fast-ID in August 2024. We, a community based in Taiwan, found no rule from Taiwan's financial regulators requiring passkeys.

According to the response, as of 18 October most consumer sites do not require attestation, and people already using synced passkeys can sign in as before. Under NIST's guidelines, a fake site cannot obtain reusable sign-in credentials when a properly configured passkey is used. The account's existing password and codes can still be phished, and according to Google's help page, adding a passkey does not remove existing verification methods. People worried about being tied to one platform can choose a password manager that exports passkeys directly.

People concerned about attestation can compare two approaches. According to the response, synced passkeys provide no attestation, while each YubiKey ships with an attestation certificate signed by Yubico.

NIST recommends that services let users register more than one authenticator for recovery; by our inference, for users this means keeping two or more ways to sign in or recover an account. According to Microsoft's help page, a passkey stored on only one device is lost if that device goes missing and there is no other recovery method.

item.title: Zero-click spyware delivered through targeted ads
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Citizen Lab published a report on 15 October linking, with high confidence, attacks on at least 45 Al Jazeera devices between 2024 and 2025 to targeted ads from the Israeli ad firm Discover-Tech and spyware from Candiru. Al Jazeera is the only confirmed target, and the exploited vulnerabilities are not described. The advice for general readers is to block ads and limit advertising IDs, which according to the report lowers only part of the risk.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 18 sources, including Citizen Lab, IAB Europe, Adtimizer

Online ads from the Israeli ad firm Discover-Tech were used to deliver mercenary spyware, the commercial spyware sold to government clients, and an ad only had to appear on screen to trigger it, according to Citizen Lab's AdFection report published on 15 October. Citizen Lab links attacks on Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025 with high confidence to spyware from the Israeli vendor Candiru, with at least 45 devices targeted. Al Jazeera is the only confirmed target in the report, while Discover-Tech's ads appeared on nearly 200,000 websites and apps, and an ad impression on its own does not mean someone was targeted. The exploited vulnerabilities and affected versions are not described, the sample the researchers obtained was a Windows executable isolated from one victim's device, and the report does not confirm that any phone was infected.

Most online ads are sold through real-time bidding (RTB), an auction held each time an ad is about to be shown, in which advertisers bid to show a given ad to a particular user, and an ad can carry code that runs inside an app or browser. According to the report, many Discover-Tech ads carried a tag that, when displayed, connected back to the company's server and sent the user's advertising ID or cookie ID. The server returned code only for chosen targets, which customers of Discover-Tech's platform could select by a phone's advertising ID, a browser's cookie ID or an IP address, and everyone else received an empty response; in the report's assessment, those customers include spyware vendors such as Candiru. Per the report, this design meant Discover-Tech never had to hand the malicious code, or even a link to it, to the platforms that ran its ads.

The researchers found two world-readable databases on Discover-Tech's website holding about 3.77 billion bid records from March to June 2026, of which about 440 million appear to have been won. At least 720 million of the bids were for ads that, judging by their names, carried a tag connecting back to these servers, and more than 70 percent of all the bids were in apps. The networks where the ads were shown, as listed in the report, include those of NATO, the United Nations, the European Parliament and the governments of more than 20 countries. In Citizen Lab's assessment, these impressions at least let Discover-Tech profile the devices and in some cases may have let other vendors' code run on them, but an impression is not confirmation of targeting or infection.

According to the companies' replies attached to the report, Google ended Discover-Tech's bidding and ad serving on its ad exchange and uses Safe Browsing to show warnings for known domains. Beeswax, Vungle (Liftoff) and Eskimi also stopped or paused their work with the company. According to IAB Europe's letter, Discover-Tech has been suspended since 8 October from the vendor list (GVL) of its Transparency and Consent Framework after an audit found breaches of framework policy, while the report's main text describes it as removed. Discover-Tech and Candiru did not respond by the report's deadline, and as of 18 October we could find no public statement from either.

Two more companies, Adtimizer and Volasim, are named in the report. Adtimizer's reply states that it only assigned some subdomains for general advertising use and that those subdomains were used only within Discover-Tech's infrastructure. Volasim's reply states that Discover-Tech was one of several outside advertising agencies it hired to promote its products, and that it is willing to provide its source code for independent review under a non-disclosure agreement. Citizen Lab sees links between both firms and Discover-Tech but notes that there is no firm evidence either took part knowingly.

Perspective

The surveillance industry calls platforms that use advertising data to identify and track specific people advertising intelligence (ADINT). According to the report, a company with access to bidding data can follow one person's movement across places and networks from bid requests carrying the same identifier, and in our reading AdFection connects this kind of identification to attack code. Citizen Lab's view is that these industry vendor lists appear to rely mostly on vendors' self-declarations. IAB Europe's letter, for its part, states that being listed does not mean IAB Europe certifies that all of a company's activities comply with the GDPR, and that it has neither the capacity nor the mandate for forensic or criminal investigations.

Citizen Lab's advice for general users is to install a trusted ad-blocking browser extension, switch to a browser that blocks tracking, regularly reset the phone's advertising ID and turn off ad tracking, and block ads at the home router or through a trusted VPN service. For security staff at organisations, its judgement is that the most practical defence for now is to block targeted ads at the network's egress (the gateway), until the industry shows it can reliably stop this technique. With no exploited vulnerability named in the report, there is no way to tell which update fixes it, and Ars Technica separately advises installing updates promptly.

Rules on the data behind targeted ads vary across Asia. Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act has no provision on advertising identifiers, real-time bidding or targeted ads. Its Article 20 does require a non-government entity that markets with personal data to stop once the person objects, and to offer a way to object the first time it markets to them (we read the current text of the statute as of 18 October, not its enforcement rules or regulators' interpretations; amendments passed on 11 November 2025 take effect on a date the Executive Yuan has yet to set). South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission published a policy plan on 31 January 2024 to protect the online behavioural data used in targeted ads, though as of 18 October we could not find whether its revised guidelines are in force.

Japan amended its Telecommunications Business Act in June 2022. According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications page, which shows no update date, websites and apps that send user data to outside parties through tags or information-collection modules must give notice of what is sent, publish it, obtain consent or offer a way to stop it. The rule does not ban targeted ads, and it covers online information services such as messaging, social media, search and news rather than corporate websites or personal blogs. In mainland China, the censorship-monitoring project GreatFire found Citizen Lab's own site, citizenlab.ca, where the report is published, fully blocked in tests up to 16 October, based on the last two conclusive tests, with interference recorded since 20 July 2017.

Citizen Lab advises people at higher risk because of their work or identity to seek expert help. Everyone else can start by limiting advertising IDs. On iPhone, go to Settings → Privacy & Security → Tracking and turn off Allow Apps to Request to Track (iOS 14.5 or later). On Android, Google's instructions are Settings → Privacy → Ads → Delete Advertising ID (this requires Google Play services), and we checked both companies' help pages on 18 October.

According to the report, these steps lower only part of the risk. In its advice to organisational security staff, Citizen Lab notes that blocking advertising IDs stops Discover-Tech's current method, but the researchers suspect this kind of attack reaches further. In our reading, resetting a phone's advertising ID does nothing against targets picked by cookie ID or IP address. The vulnerabilities have not been disclosed, so there is no way to tell which update would fix them.

item.title: Tuta encrypted email and its Nextcloud integration
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Tuta and Nextcloud launched an integration on 1 October that lets you use Tuta inside Nextcloud, save received attachments to Nextcloud and create Nextcloud Talk meeting links from Tuta Calendar. A Nextcloud administrator has to install the app, and as of 18 October neither announcement explains how attachments are protected once they are in Nextcloud.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including Tuta, Nextcloud, CyberInsider

Encrypted email service Tuta and the open-source collaboration platform Nextcloud launched an integration on 1 October, which Tuta's announcement describes as free. It has two parts: a Tuta Mail app in the Nextcloud App Store that runs Tuta's web client inside Nextcloud, and a Nextcloud plugin in Tuta that saves received attachments to Nextcloud with one click or creates a Nextcloud Talk meeting link when you set up a Tuta Calendar event. Both features need the Tuta Mail app on your own Nextcloud; the App Store page lists Nextcloud 33 to 35. On a self-hosted server the administrator installs it, and on a managed one the provider has to make it available.

According to Tuta's announcement, the account administrator enables the plugin for all users under Settings → Plugins, and a single user is their own administrator. Tuta's README on GitHub lists two settings, the Nextcloud address and the folder for attachments, and the features work inside Nextcloud as well as in Tuta's web, desktop and mobile clients. Per Nextcloud's press release, the integration makes it easier for individuals and small businesses to self-host Nextcloud while leaving email to Tuta.

As of 18 October, neither Tuta's announcement nor its pricing page says which plan is required. Tuta's apps have a Traditional Chinese interface. In Tuta's public source code as of 18 October, the Traditional Chinese language file covers the general Plugins page, while the Nextcloud plugin's own settings and buttons such as "Save to Nextcloud" exist only in English and German.

Perspective

Tuta's encryption page says emails, including subject lines and all attachments, are end-to-end encrypted and the key is never shared with anyone, Tuta included. Neither announcement explains what happens to that protection once an attachment is saved to Nextcloud, so we read Tuta's public source code as of 18 October. The save button sits in the attachment-saving dialog, and the plugin uploads through Nextcloud's file access interface (WebDAV) without any extra encryption. Our inference is that the uploaded file is the decrypted one, and it leaves Tuta's end-to-end encryption when it reaches Nextcloud.

Nextcloud's administration manual distinguishes two kinds of encryption. Server-side encryption runs on the server with keys stored there, and the manual warns that it does not protect against a compromised server or a malicious administrator. End-to-end encryption is done by Nextcloud's desktop or mobile clients before upload. Because the plugin does not upload through those clients, how well an attachment is protected on Nextcloud depends on that server's settings and who runs it, which is our inference from the manual and the code.

For Talk, the source code shows the plugin creating a public conversation, which Talk's API documentation lists as one that allows guests. Nextcloud's product page says Talk supports end-to-end encrypted calls in the web and new desktop clients, without saying whether public conversations are covered.

In mainland China, the third-party monitor GreatFire rates tuta.com as intermittently disrupted, with 59% of the last 17 conclusive tests up to 11 October showing interference. In India, the Internet Freedom Foundation noted reports that 14 end-to-end encrypted and peer-to-peer messaging apps, not email services, were banned in May 2023 without a published order. In April 2025 the Karnataka High Court ordered central authorities to act to block Proton Mail, though MediaNama noted that Proton Mail was still reachable in India when it reported the order. We found no reports of Tuta itself being blocked in India.

People or teams already using Nextcloud and Tuta can have the Nextcloud administrator install the Tuta Mail app, then have the Tuta account administrator enable the plugin. The manual notes that server-side encryption does not protect against the server's administrators, so before saving sensitive attachments it is worth checking who has administrative access to that server. Based on the source code and Talk's documentation, the plugin creates public conversations that allow guests, so anyone with the link can join as a guest.
